nodes.question: What technique is used to observe internal crack propagation in concrete?
nodes.answer: X-ray Computed Tomography Scanning (X-ray CT scanning) is used to observe internal crack propagation.
nodes.paragraph: Digital Image Correlation (DIC) can Materials and Structures (2025) 58:74 74 Vol. : (123456789) supplement these tests, providing an estimate of the displacement fields and making crack propagation on concrete surfaces visible [4 , 24]. Regarding the meso-scale, observing internal crack propagation is crucial in understanding the nature of frost damage inside the concrete. With this aim, X-ray Computed Tomography Scanning (X-ray CT scanning) is a non-destructive technique capable of distinguish- ing aggregates from cement paste [32 34] and highlighting internal cracks [29, 35 38]. However, studies combining DIC for macro-scale fracture behaviour and X-ray CT imaging for meso-scale crack propagation are lacking. This is particularly true for research on the interaction between pre- damage, water boundary conditions, and internal frost damage in concrete. This experimental study aims to investigate the interaction between pre-damage, water boundary conditions and internal frost damage at dual-scale. Concrete specimens were pre-damaged under ten- sion or compression and thereafter subjected to various water boundary conditions during FTCs. Electronic probes embedded in the concrete moni- tored temperature changes throughout the FTC procedure.

nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: How is the contrast in an X-ray radiograph determined?
nodes.answer: The contrast between different regions in an X-ray radiograph or CT image is directly correlated to the X-ray attenuation through that region of the sample.
nodes.paragraph: XCT, a nondestructive technique, can provide surface and volumetric information on samples. 31 Originating in the 1960s, the computed tomography technique was recognized with the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1979.32XCT passes a collimated beam of X-rays through a sample where the resulting radiograph, which is a two-dimensional (2D) map of X-ray attenuation, is captured by a detector locatedon the opposite side of the sample from the X-ray source. The contrast between different regions in an X-ray radiograph or CT image is directly correlatedto the X-ray attenuation through that region of the sample. This X-ray attenuation is determined with the Beer Lambert law, 33shown in Eq. 1, where u(t) is the photon ux at the detector plane, B(E,t) is the buildup factor which accounts scattered photons in the material, u0is the initial photon ux, Ris the macroscopic cross section of the sample material,and tis the thickness of the sample. The buildup factor represents beam hardening and other buildup effects caused by photon scattering which maycreate artifacts in reconstructions that need to be addressed via post-processing methods.

nodes.answer: The work describes the post-irradiation examination capabilities of X-ray computed tomography at INL.
nodes.paragraph: This work describes the X- ray computed tomography post-irradiation examination capabilities at INL, aswell as detailing a variety of applications this instrument has examined. nodes.question: What is XCT and what information does it provide?
nodes.answer: XCT, or X-ray computed tomography, is a nondestructive technique that provides surface and volumetric information on samples.
nodes.paragraph: XCT, a nondestructive technique, can provide surface and volumetric information on samples. 31 Originating in the 1960s, the computed tomography technique was recognized with the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1979.32XCT passes a collimated beam of X-rays through a sample where the resulting radiograph, which is a two-dimensional (2D) map of X-ray attenuation, is captured by a detector locatedon the opposite side of the sample from the X-ray source. The contrast between different regions in an X-ray radiograph or CT image is directly correlatedto the X-ray attenuation through that region of the sample. This X-ray attenuation is determined with the Beer Lambert law, 33shown in Eq. 1, where u(t) is the photon ux at the detector plane, B(E,t) is the buildup factor which accounts scattered photons in the material, u0is the initial photon ux, Ris the macroscopic cross section of the sample material,and tis the thickness of the sample. The buildup factor represents beam hardening and other buildup effects caused by photon scattering which maycreate artifacts in reconstructions that need to be addressed via post-processing methods.

nodes.question: What is the primary function of XCT as described in the paragraph?
nodes.answer: XCT collects a series of radiographs based on sample rotation and reconstructs them mathematically to produce a three-dimensional (3D) dataset.
nodes.paragraph: In XCT, a series of radiographs are collected as a function ofsample rotation and then are mathematically recon-structed to produce a three-dimensional (3D) dataset. 34ut BE ;t /C2 u0e/COR/C1t 1 As the name implies, laboratory-based XCT sys- items can be installed as a standalone system in a laboratory as opposed to using larger facilities such as synchrotron sources. Micro-XCT, which providessub-millimeter and even sub-micron XCT to exam- line samples physical properties and morphological composition, has become more available due toengineering and technological advances. Theseadvances 35 38include scintillator-coated micro- scopes and improvements in X-ray sources to reduce the X-ray spot size, both of which increase theachievable spatial resolution of the system. The introduction of micro-XCT as a routine capability in the PIE process has enabled XCT to provide deeperinsights into fundamental material science phenomena. The laboratory-based micro-XCT at IMCL is particularly useful for quantifying voids and cracks in samples, examining internal interfaces between different structures or materials within specimens, ,measuring surface roughness, and identifying post-test sample changes in regimes spanning from the engineering scale to the microscale. When inte- grated with other examination techniques, XCT canhelp enable correlative microscopy which can provide information on a sample from the engineer- ing length scale down to the atomic level.

nodes.question: What software is installed on the Xradia 620 Versa to aid in image reconstruction?
nodes.answer: The ZEISS Scout-and-Scan Control System Reconstructor software is installed for performing preliminary reconstructions from radiographic datasets.
nodes.paragraph: The ZEISS Scout-and-Scan technology canallow for a low-resolution, large FOV scan to rst be conducted, and then regions of interest can be zoomed-in on and a high-resolution scan can betaken of a sub-volume of the sample to reveal more detail. The X-ray source applies a voltage, which can vary from 30 to 160 kVp, to a tungsten target to produce a Bremsstrahlung X-ray spectrum in a cone-beam geometry with maximum energies thatcan range from 30 to 160 keV. In September 2023, this instrument was upgraded to the ZEISS Xradia 620 Versa, shown in Fig. 1, which provided an upgraded source, increasing the X-ray source powerfrom 10 to 25 W, while keeping the X-ray energy range the same. This upgrade reduces imaging time by approximately a factor of 2 while also improvingthe detection statistics for high-resolution imaging. Computational Resources The Xradia 620 Versa is equipped with a work- station containing a Xeon processor clocked at 2.20 GHz, which helps with data collection and perform preliminary image reconstruction, a pro-cess which converts the 2D radiographs to 3Dvolumetric data. This machine has the ZEISS Scout-and-Scan Control System Reconstructor soft- ware installed in it which can perform preliminaryreconstructions from radiographic datasets.

nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What is the expected growth of CT and MR imaging emissions between 2016 and 2030?
nodes.answer: It is expected that CT and MR imaging emissions will grow by 30% between 2016 and 2030.
nodes.paragraph: As healthcare professionals, wecan protect our patients by responding to the health effects of climate change and other environmental expo- sures and signal the importance of an urgent transition to environmentally sustainable imaging practice [ 3]. The delivery of healthcare generates substantial greenhousegas emissions, with diagnostic services accounting forapproximately 9% of healthcare emissions in one region inAustralia [ 4]. Globally, CT and MR imaging were esti- mated to contribute up to 0.77% of total carbon dioxideemissions for 2016 with an expected 30% growth between 2016 and 2030 [ 5,6]. For comparison, aviation con- tributed an estimated 2.5% worldwide in 2023 [ 7].Rockall et al .European Radiology Transformation of medical imaging to low-carbon and climate-resilient systems will require engagement at all organizational levels locally and globally, and at a societallevel. Individual radiologists and radiology practices can actas agents for change in their daily practice and within theirhealthcare organizations. Radiological societies may con-tribute by in uencing not only our community but also government policy. We must consider the environmentalimpact of our daily work, balancing responsible imaging usage against the immediate needs of patients.
